title: Symptomatic Bradycardia: Treat the Patient, Not the Number
bottomLine: A slow heart rate requires emergency treatment when it causes hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic chest discomfort, shock, or acute heart failure. Assess reversible causes, support ABCs, and prepare for atropine and pacing/vasoactive therapy according to the emergency algorithm.
recognize: Bradycardia can be caused by conduction disease, ischemia, hypoxia, electrolyte problems, medications, hypothermia, or increased vagal tone.
A low rate without poor perfusion may not need immediate drug treatment.
High-grade AV block can deteriorate suddenly.
priorities: Assess airway, breathing, blood pressure, perfusion, mental status, chest pain, and heart-failure signs.
Obtain rhythm monitoring/12-lead ECG when available without delaying stabilization.
Activate emergency response for symptomatic instability and prepare for ordered atropine, transcutaneous pacing, or infusion therapy.
assessMonitor: Trend rhythm, rate, blood pressure, level of consciousness, oxygenation, chest symptoms, electrolytes, and medication exposures.
interventions: Apply pacing pads early when high-grade block or deterioration is likely.
Treat reversible causes such as hypoxia or medication toxicity as directed.
medicationSafety: Beta blockers, certain calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, and other agents can worsen bradycardia.
Atropine may be ineffective in some high-grade conduction blocks; do not delay pacing when the patient remains unstable.
teaching: Report fainting, severe dizziness, chest pain, or worsening exercise intolerance, especially after medication changes.
delegationScope: Routine pulse measurement may be delegated in stable patients; interpretation of symptomatic bradycardia requires licensed-nurse assessment and immediate escalation.
examTrap: Treating every heart rate below 60 with atropine even when the patient is asymptomatic and perfusing normally.
oneLinePearl: Bradycardia becomes an emergency when perfusion fails.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support Guidelines

title: Supraventricular Tachycardia: Stability Before Rate
bottomLine: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia may be SVT, but the first question is whether the patient is stable. Hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic chest pain, shock, or acute heart failure requires immediate synchronized-cardioversion pathway escalation.
recognize: SVT often has abrupt onset/offset with a rapid regular pulse, palpitations, dizziness, dyspnea, or chest discomfort.
Sinus tachycardia usually has an underlying driver such as fever, pain, dehydration, hypoxia, or anxiety that must be treated.
Wide-complex tachycardia should not be casually treated as SVT.
priorities: Assess ABCs, blood pressure, perfusion, chest symptoms, mental status, and rhythm characteristics.
For stable regular narrow-complex SVT, support ordered vagal maneuvers and adenosine protocol.
For instability, activate synchronized-cardioversion response immediately.
assessMonitor: Continuous ECG/rhythm monitoring during acute treatment; trend BP, oxygenation, symptoms, potassium/magnesium, and recurrence.
interventions: Use only safe, instructed vagal techniques.
Capture a 12-lead ECG when possible before/after conversion without delaying emergency treatment.
medicationSafety: Adenosine can cause brief flushing, chest pressure, dyspnea, and transient asystole; administer via the prescribed rapid IV technique with monitoring.
Avoid carotid sinus massage in routine nursing practice unless specifically directed by an appropriately qualified clinician.
teaching: Report recurrent palpitations with syncope, chest pain, or dyspnea and follow cardiology guidance on triggers and recurrence.
delegationScope: Acute tachyarrhythmia assessment and emergency medication response require licensed-nurse competency and escalation.
examTrap: Focusing on slowing a fast rate before checking whether the patient is unstable.
oneLinePearl: SVT: stable or unstable comes before the medication name.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support Guidelines

title: Pacemakers: Capture, Sensing, and Patient Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A pacemaker must both sense intrinsic cardiac activity appropriately and capture the myocardium when it fires. New dizziness, syncope, bradycardia, pacing spikes without QRS complexes, or infection at the device pocket requires prompt evaluation.
recognize: Failure to capture appears as a pacing spike not followed by the expected depolarization.
Failure to sense can cause inappropriate pacing relative to intrinsic beats.
Pocket redness, drainage, fever, or erosion can indicate device infection.
priorities: Assess the patient first—perfusion, symptoms, pulse, rhythm, and blood pressure.
Use telemetry/ECG to compare pacing spikes with cardiac response.
Escalate symptomatic device malfunction immediately and prepare external pacing support if needed.
assessMonitor: Trend rhythm, pulse, symptoms, incision/pocket site, fever, and postimplant mobility instructions.
interventions: After implantation, protect the incision and follow device-specific arm/activity restrictions.
Maintain accurate device identification and communicate pacemaker status before procedures involving electromagnetic equipment.
medicationSafety: Medication-induced bradycardia can still occur in paced patients depending on device settings and underlying rhythm.
MRI compatibility and procedural precautions are device specific; never assume all pacemakers have the same restrictions.
teaching: Carry device identification and report syncope, persistent hiccups/muscle twitching, fever, drainage, or new palpitations.
delegationScope: Routine incision care may be delegated when stable; rhythm/device malfunction assessment requires licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Assuming a visible pacer spike means the pacemaker is functioning correctly without verifying capture and patient perfusion.
oneLinePearl: A pacer spike only matters if the heart responds.
sourceBasis: ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay Guideline
FDA implanted cardiac device safety information

title: Valvular Disease: Congestion, Syncope, and Perfusion
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Valvular disease becomes clinically important when it impairs forward flow or causes congestion. New exertional syncope, angina, worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, or reduced perfusion requires reassessment rather than routine symptom management alone.
recognize: Aortic stenosis classically can cause exertional dyspnea, angina, and syncope.
Mitral disease may contribute to pulmonary congestion and atrial fibrillation.
Murmur intensity alone does not reliably measure severity.
priorities: Assess activity tolerance, chest pain, syncope, respiratory symptoms, edema, rhythm, and perfusion.
Monitor for new atrial fibrillation or heart-failure signs.
Escalate syncope, acute pulmonary edema, ischemic symptoms, or hypotension.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, edema, lung sounds, oxygenation, BP, rhythm, and echocardiography follow-up status.
interventions: Support sodium/fluid and activity plans when prescribed.
Prepare patients for valve intervention evaluation when symptoms/severity warrant.
medicationSafety: Preload- and afterload-altering drugs can have different effects depending on the valve lesion; follow the disease-specific plan rather than assuming all murmurs are treated alike.
Anticoagulation may be required for atrial fibrillation or selected prosthetic valves and needs bleeding monitoring.
teaching: Report worsening exertional symptoms and keep echocardiography/cardiology follow-up even when symptoms are gradual.
delegationScope: Routine weights may be delegated; new syncope, dyspnea, or rhythm changes require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Treating a new exertional fainting episode as simple dehydration in a patient with known severe aortic stenosis.
oneLinePearl: Valve disease becomes urgent when flow fails: syncope, chest pain, congestion, poor perfusion.
sourceBasis: ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease

title: Hypertensive Emergency: Look for Acute Organ Injury
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A very high blood pressure becomes a hypertensive emergency when acute target-organ injury is present. Neurologic deficits, encephalopathy, ACS, pulmonary edema, aortic syndrome, acute kidney injury, retinal emergency, or pregnancy-related severe features require immediate higher-level care.
recognize: Headache alone does not define hypertensive emergency; acute organ injury does.
Pain, anxiety, missed medications, or measurement error can cause severe readings without emergency injury.
Rapid uncontrolled BP reduction can impair cerebral, coronary, or renal perfusion.
priorities: Repeat BP with correct technique while assessing neurologic, cardiac, respiratory, renal, vascular, and pregnancy/postpartum symptoms.
Activate emergency evaluation when target-organ injury is suspected.
Prepare for monitored IV therapy when ordered rather than attempting rapid normalization with unsupervised oral medication.
assessMonitor: Frequent BP, neurologic status, ECG/rhythm, oxygenation, urine output, chest/back pain, and treatment response.
interventions: Maintain a calm monitored environment and address reversible triggers while emergency diagnostics proceed.
Use syndrome-specific BP goals and medications under provider direction.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly lower BP to normal in most hypertensive emergencies unless a syndrome-specific protocol requires a different target.
Pregnancy/postpartum severe hypertension uses obstetric-specific pathways.
teaching: Severe BP plus chest pain, neurologic symptoms, dyspnea, or pregnancy warning signs requires emergency care.
delegationScope: Repeat BP measurement may be delegated with immediate reporting thresholds; target-organ assessment requires licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Trying to normalize a very high BP rapidly before determining whether acute organ injury is present.
oneLinePearl: Hypertensive emergency = high BP plus acute organ damage.

title: Tension Pneumothorax: Do Not Wait for the X-Ray
bottomLine: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical emergency caused by rising intrathoracic pressure that impairs ventilation and venous return. Severe respiratory distress, unilateral absent breath sounds, hypotension, and obstructive-shock signs require immediate decompression response without waiting for confirmatory imaging.
recognize: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea can occur after trauma, procedures, positive-pressure ventilation, or spontaneous pneumothorax.
Distended neck veins may occur but can be absent in hypovolemia.
Tracheal deviation is a late and unreliable finding.
priorities: Activate emergency response and assess ABCs immediately.
Provide high-concentration oxygen when hypoxemic/distressed and prepare for needle/finger decompression by the qualified provider followed by chest tube placement.
Do not transport an unstable patient for routine imaging before decompression.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory effort, breath sounds, oxygenation, BP, pulse, mental status, and response after decompression.
interventions: After chest tube placement, manage the drainage system safely and monitor for recurrence or ongoing air leak.
medicationSafety: Positive-pressure ventilation can worsen an untreated tension pneumothorax; airway support must be coordinated with immediate decompression.
redFlags: Hypotension with unilateral absent breath sounds
teaching: After recovery, report recurrent sudden chest pain or dyspnea immediately.
delegationScope: This is an emergency requiring immediate licensed-nurse recognition and escalation; routine respiratory tasks must not delay decompression.
examTrap: Sending an unstable patient for chest x-ray before treating a clinically obvious tension pneumothorax.
oneLinePearl: Tension pneumothorax is treated on the bedside pattern, not the x-ray result.
sourceBasis: American College of Surgeons ATLS principles

title: ARDS: Severe Hypoxemia and Lung-Protective Support
bottomLine: ARDS is acute inflammatory lung injury with severe oxygenation impairment not fully explained by cardiac failure. PN care in critical settings focuses on oxygenation, ventilator-associated safety, prone-position support, fluid balance, skin protection, sedation assessment, and rapid escalation of deterioration.
recognize: ARDS often follows sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, major trauma, or pancreatitis.
Patients can develop rapidly worsening hypoxemia, tachypnea, diffuse bilateral infiltrates, and increased work of breathing.
Oxygenation may remain poor despite supplemental oxygen.
priorities: Assess oxygenation, work of breathing, hemodynamics, mental status, and ventilator response.
Support lung-protective ventilation and PEEP strategies ordered by the critical-care team.
Escalate sudden desaturation, hypotension, or ventilator alarms after immediate bedside checks.
assessMonitor: Trend SpO2/ABGs when ordered, ventilator pressures, breath sounds, fluid balance, urine output, sedation, skin, and prone-position complications.
interventions: Use meticulous oral care, VTE prevention, pressure-injury prevention, and early mobility when feasible.
During prone positioning, protect airway devices, eyes, pressure points, and lines.
medicationSafety: Deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade may be used selectively and requires continuous respiratory/hemodynamic safety monitoring.
Avoid reflexive large fluid loads after initial shock resuscitation when a conservative fluid strategy is prescribed.
teaching: Explain critical-care positioning and ventilator strategies to family in simple terms when appropriate.
delegationScope: ARDS patients are unstable/critical; tasks require close RN/critical-care oversight and facility-defined LPN/LVN scope.
examTrap: Assuming worsening hypoxemia is simply pneumonia progression without checking tube position, pneumothorax, secretions, or hemodynamic change.
oneLinePearl: ARDS care protects oxygenation while protecting the lungs from the ventilator.
sourceBasis: American Thoracic Society ARDS Clinical Practice Guidance

title: Pleural Effusion: Fluid Around the Lung
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pleural effusion compresses lung tissue and may reflect heart failure, infection, malignancy, or other disease. Increasing dyspnea, hypoxemia, fever, or hemodynamic compromise requires reassessment and possible drainage/diagnostic evaluation.
recognize: Decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, dyspnea, cough, and pleuritic discomfort can occur.
A large effusion can cause significant respiratory compromise.
Infected pleural fluid/empyema often occurs with fever and systemic illness.
priorities: Assess respiratory effort, oxygenation, breath sounds, fever, pain, and underlying disease signs.
Position upright as tolerated and administer oxygen for hypoxemia.
Prepare for thoracentesis or drainage when ordered.
assessMonitor: Trend oxygenation, respiratory rate, breath sounds, temperature, fluid balance, imaging results, and response after drainage.
interventions: For thoracentesis, position and monitor the patient according to procedure protocol.
After drainage, watch for pneumothorax, bleeding, cough, or respiratory deterioration.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet status should be reviewed before invasive pleural procedures according to protocol.
Diuretics may help heart-failure effusions but do not treat all causes.
redFlags: New unilateral absent breath sounds after thoracentesis
teaching: Report worsening breathlessness, fever, or chest pain after a pleural procedure.
delegationScope: Routine positioning may be delegated; respiratory deterioration and postprocedure complications require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming every pleural effusion should be treated with diuretics without considering infection or malignancy.
oneLinePearl: Pleural effusion is a finding—treat the cause and watch breathing.
sourceBasis: American Thoracic Society pleural disease guidance

title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Airborne Isolation and Treatment Adherence
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires prompt airborne precautions and public-health coordination. Active TB disease is not the same as latent TB infection; treatment uses multidrug therapy with adherence and toxicity monitoring.
recognize: Pulmonary TB can cause prolonged cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, fever, night sweats, fatigue, weight loss, and poor appetite.
Latent TB infection has no symptoms and is not contagious.
TB can also involve the brain, spine, kidneys, and other organs.
priorities: Place suspected infectious pulmonary TB in airborne isolation according to facility protocol and use a fit-tested respirator.
Collect ordered sputum specimens using correct airborne precautions.
Notify infection prevention and the appropriate state/local public-health program.
assessMonitor: Trend symptoms, weight, adherence, liver/vision or other drug-specific adverse effects, sputum results, and isolation-clearance criteria.
interventions: Support directly observed therapy or video DOT when arranged by the TB program.
Use medication calendars and social-support resources to improve completion.
medicationSafety: Isoniazid, rifamycins, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol have important drug-specific toxicities and interactions; monitor according to the regimen.
Report jaundice, severe nausea, visual change, neuropathy, or other serious adverse effects promptly.
teaching: Treatment completion protects both the patient and the community; follow the TB program's isolation and medication plan exactly.
delegationScope: Isolation procedures may be shared with trained staff, but medication toxicity, respiratory deterioration, and public-health reporting require licensed clinical oversight.
examTrap: Using a surgical mask instead of a fit-tested respirator when entering the room of a patient with suspected infectious pulmonary TB.
oneLinePearl: Active pulmonary TB: airborne isolation, multidrug therapy, public-health partnership.
sourceBasis: CDC 2025 Clinical Overview of Tuberculosis Disease

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Airway Collapse and Sedation Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Obstructive sleep apnea causes repeated upper-airway collapse during sleep and increases daytime sleepiness, cardiometabolic risk, and perioperative respiratory vulnerability. Consistent positive-airway-pressure therapy and caution with sedatives/opioids are high-yield nursing priorities.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas/gasping, morning headaches, nonrestorative sleep, and daytime sleepiness are common clues.
Obesity increases risk but OSA can occur at any body size.
Untreated OSA increases postoperative and opioid-related respiratory risk.
priorities: Assess home CPAP/BiPAP use, daytime somnolence, perioperative plan, opioid/sedative exposure, and oxygenation/respiratory status.
Ensure prescribed PAP equipment is available and used correctly during hospitalization when appropriate.
Escalate recurrent apnea, severe desaturation, or oversedation.
assessMonitor: Trend sedation level, respiratory rate, oxygenation, PAP tolerance, sleep quality, and adherence barriers.
interventions: Promote weight management, side sleeping, and avoidance of alcohol/sedative misuse when clinically appropriate.
Use enhanced respiratory monitoring after anesthesia/opioids when ordered for high-risk patients.
medicationSafety: Opioids, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives can worsen upper-airway obstruction and hypoventilation.
Supplemental oxygen may improve saturation but does not correct airway obstruction; continue PAP/airway management as prescribed.
teaching: Use PAP consistently, bring the device for procedures when instructed, and avoid driving when dangerously sleepy.
delegationScope: Routine device setup may be assisted by trained staff; oversedation or apnea requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming normal awake oxygen saturation means a patient with severe OSA has no opioid-related respiratory risk.
oneLinePearl: OSA is an airway problem—oxygen alone does not splint the airway open.
sourceBasis: American Society of Anesthesiologists perioperative OSA principles
